newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU farm ministers discuss beef crisis measures.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers discuss beef crisis measures.

text.p: European Union agriculture ministers on Tuesday discussed ways to compensate angry farmers for a beef price slump caused by the mad cow crisis that has isolated Britain from its partners.

Thousands of dairy farmers descended on the ministers' rural conference hotel, demanding action to help them deal with a collapse of their crucial beef export market which they blame firmly on Britain.
"We're being blackenend by the British brush," said Limerick farmer John Sparling.

Robert Ruttle, now back in business in Limerick after being "cleaned out" by mad cow disease in 1993, called on Britain to go ahead with an extra cull of cattle at risk from Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).

"Britain Scuttles (our beef) Enterprise," proclaimed one banner carried by nearly three thousand farmers braving rain outside the meeting. Organisers expected a total of six thousand from across all Ireland by the day's end.

At the talks ministers were expected to put pressure on Britain's Minister Douglas Hogg to explain his government's suspension of part of a cattle cull, supposed to eradicate the disease in Britain and restore confidence in the meat.

They are refusing to lift a worldwide ban on British beef until the London government carries out in full a plan drawn up at an EU summit in Florence last June and are angry at what they see as a U-turn by Prime Minister John Major.
The protest is timed to coincide with discussion of measures to restore confidence in beef and to compensate farmers for a sharp drop in household consumption of beef and in farmers' income.

Eight out of 10 Irish cattle are exported and the Irish farming lobby says the mad cow scare has tainted the meat market worldwide and led to traditional customers in the Middle East and elsehwere shunning Irish beef.
Ministers are expected to call for a major expansion of a fund to promote beef consumption both in the EU and world markets to put a floor under falling beef prices.
At present the fund amounts to some 10 million Ecus ($12 million) and EU officials said it could be increased as much as five-fold.
Ministers are also expected to bring forward aid payments to beef farmers from the 1997 budget to the current budget which could make a further 500 million Ecus available in compensation this year.
This would be in addition to some 850 million Ecus made available in emergency aid funds so far since the crisis erupted in March this year.
Officials said the meeting might also agree to buy more surplus beef from the market to stop prices collapsing. The beef is frozen in EU storage for export.

Britain has come in for sharp criticism from its European partners for announcing last week that new scientific evidence showed the slaughter of up to 147,000 young cattle agreed in Florence would not speed up the eradication of BSE.
It suspended plans to carry out the cull but is going ahead with the slaughter of up to one million older cattle a year to try to stamp out BSE.
